summary:
New York sits in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and withdrawal of legal recognition. The same ranking places the least protective states at the opposite end, with prison terms of up to five years for youth-care provision and arrest policies for gender-identity bathroom use.

Gender identity and expression have been protected statewide in credit, housing, employment, education and public accommodations since the Gender Expression Non-Discrimination Act was signed in January 2019 and took effect in February 2019, building on a 2009 executive order barring gender-identity discrimination in state employment and Division of Human Rights regulations issued 4 November 2015, effective 20 January 2016, covering transgender harassment and discrimination in those domains. A 2024 constitutional amendment explicitly bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity.

The Hate Crimes Act has covered gender identity and expression since 1 November 2019, with further anti-bias reform bills signed in November 2022. The gay and transgender panic defence was repealed in June 2019, effective immediately, making New York the sixth state to abolish it. Conversion therapy on minors has been banned effective 25 January 2019.

Since 2014 transgender adults could change the gender on birth certificates with a notarized medical affidavit verifying surgery or a gender dysphoria diagnosis; this was updated in 2020 to allow self-affirmation, with parental consent required for those under 17. The June 2021 Gender Recognition Act allowed an X marker on driver's licences and eased sealing of name- and gender-change records. An X marker on New York City birth certificates took effect 1 January 2019 and on death certificates from 2 January 2020; X was reported for state court and jury documents in November 2019 and in healthcare data from August 2020; X on all state forms was approved in April 2022 for 2023, with some organizations until 2024, alongside updatable marriage certificates. A November 2021 law effective 1 January 2022 requires utilities and municipalities to use preferred names and pronouns.

Shield protections apply. The MAP Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, data as of 27 September 2026, lists New York as a state with a shield law or executive order from 2023: the shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care legal in New York was banned in their home state, which is directly relevant to visitors travelling from ban states. Nationally, 16 states and the District of Columbia, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, hold shields, while 32 states and five territories, covering 56%, hold none. New York City issued an executive order on 12 June 2023 barring city resources from being used to detain, prosecute or investigate the provision or receipt of gender-affirming care. A state law of 25 June 2023, making New York the twelfth shield state, bars courts from enforcing out-of-state laws removing custody over youth gender-affirming care, bars treating such care as child abuse, and bars law-enforcement cooperation with out-of-state agencies. A September 2023 Ithaca ordinance and April 2025 City Council bills expanded provider protections.

Former Penal Law Section 240.37, in effect since 1976 and used by police to harass and arrest transgender individuals, was repealed in February 2021, effective immediately. Gender-neutral bathrooms were mandated by a law signed in December 2020, effective 23 March 2021. The anti-bullying law covers gender, including gender identity and expression, including cyberbullying, in all public elementary and secondary schools, with a 2019 loophole closure. A June 2023 law explicitly includes gender identity in drug treatment and addiction programmes, and a November 2020 law requires annual judiciary statistics by gender identity.

Nassau County remains the only county in New York banning transgender athletes from women's sports on county-run facilities, with a 2025 ruling finding no clear violation of anti-discrimination laws and an NYCLU lawsuit seeking inclusion.

Same-sex marriage became legal statewide under the Marriage Equality Act, passed 24 June 2011 and effective 24 July 2011, following a May 2008 directive recognizing out-of-jurisdiction marriages. Consenting adult same-sex sexual activity was legalized by New York v. Onofre in 1980, with defunct sodomy provisions affecting National Guard employees repealed effective 2000. A 2019 law granted state veterans benefits to those dishonorably discharged under Don't Ask, Don't Tell from 1993 to 2011.

On 16 December 2009 New York barred state agencies from discriminating on the basis of gender identity in all state-employment matters including hiring, termination, retention, appointment, promotion, tenure, recruitment and compensation, defining gender identity as having or being perceived as having a gender identity, self-image, appearance, behavior or expression whether or not different from sex assigned at birth, and ordered equal-opportunity efforts, consistent guidelines and swift confidential complaint investigations, effective immediately.
tangentialFactors:
New York's protective posture operates inside a national framework that has moved sharply against trans people since January 2025. Federal passport and visa rules, federal facility mandates, federal custody policies and federal healthcare funding restrictions apply at the border and in federally controlled settings regardless of New York law; a visitor's exposure at entry, in federal buildings, or in federal custody is governed by those national rules, not by New York's statutes.

The July 2026 ranking that places New York in the Most Protective tier is a rubric over tracked bills and enacted laws, not a measure of incidents or of enforcement on the ground. Its contrast tier identifies Idaho with prison terms of up to five years and Florida with an arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use, which shows the spread of the national picture New York sits apart from.

The shield-law count is a national distribution: 16 states and the District of Columbia hold shields covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, while 32 states and five territories covering 56% hold none. New York's shield therefore protects people who travel here for care, but offers no protection once they return to a ban state.

Public-attitude polling cited in the source shows support for discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity rising from 75% in 2017, with 19% opposed, to 82% in 2022, with 14% opposed; same-sex marriage support moved from 69% in 2017 to 75% in 2022. These figures are LGBTQ-general and do not isolate transgender-specific attitudes.
localsOnly:
Residents benefit from the full stack of state protections: GENDA's statewide coverage of credit, housing, employment, education and public accommodations since February 2019, the 2009 executive order on state employment, the 2015 Division of Human Rights regulations, and the 2024 constitutional amendment barring gender-identity discrimination.

Birth-certificate gender change has been available since 2014 by notarized medical affidavit, self-affirmation since 2020 with parental consent for minors, and the June 2021 Gender Recognition Act added X markers on driver's licences and easier sealing of name- and gender-change records. X markers extend to New York City birth certificates (1 January 2019), death certificates (2 January 2020), state court and jury documents (November 2019), healthcare data (August 2020) and all state forms approved in April 2022 for 2023, with some organizations until 2024. Utilities and municipalities must use preferred names and pronouns under a law effective 1 January 2022.

The Hate Crimes Act has covered gender identity and expression since 1 November 2019, with anti-bias reform bills signed November 2022. The panic defence was repealed in June 2019. Conversion therapy on minors has been banned since 25 January 2019. Penal Law Section 240.37, used to arrest transgender people, was repealed in February 2021. Gender-neutral bathrooms have been mandated since 23 March 2021.

Shield statutes protect residents and providers: the 12 June 2023 New York City executive order, the 25 June 2023 state law barring enforcement of out-of-state custody-removal orders and law-enforcement cooperation, a September 2023 Ithaca ordinance and April 2025 City Council bills.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 24 July 2011 under the Marriage Equality Act. Adoption non-discrimination for gay and lesbian applicants dates to 1982, second-parent adoption was protected by 1995 rulings, joint same-sex adoption was allowed by 2004, though an October 2020 district court order allowed religious-affiliated agencies to turn away gay, single and unmarried heterosexual couples. Commercial surrogacy, banned from 1992 to 2020, was legalized effective February 2021, with a February 2021 requirement that insurance cover same-sex couples for IVF, surrogacy and fertility treatments, amid an April 2022 lawsuit by a male same-sex couple alleging only heterosexual and female same-sex couples receive coverage.

Nassau County bans transgender athletes from women's sports on county-run facilities; a 2025 ruling found no clear violation of anti-discrimination laws and the NYCLU has sued for inclusion.

SONDA, effective 2003, prohibits actual or perceived sexual orientation discrimination and explicitly includes asexuality. The Hate Crimes Act has covered sexual orientation since 1 July 2001. Under Yonaty v. Mincolla (30 May 2012), labeling someone gay or homosexual is no longer defamation. St. Patrick's Day parade bans ended in September 2014 in New York City and November 2024 in Staten Island. A 1985 law enabling municipalities to close gay bathhouses and saunas remains in effect as of August 2026. Adultery was repealed in November 2024.

New York City is home to the largest transgender U.S. population, estimated at 50,000 in 2018 and concentrated in Manhattan and Queens, within broader 2005 estimates of 272,493 self-identifying gay and bisexual individuals in the city and 568,903 LGB residents in the metropolitan area.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source's societal-tolerance language — that New York has "generally been seen as socially liberal" and that attitudes moved "from general antipathy and hostility to tolerance and acceptance" — refers to the LGBTQ community generally, not to transgender people specifically; the article provides no trans-specific tolerance quote distinct from LGBTQ-general wording. This is unresolved in the inventory.

The inventory does not document any trans-specific violence incident in New York, nor any figure that could be compared against a general New York homicide rate, so no trans-specific violence magnitude can be stated here.

The 2018 estimate of 50,000 transgender residents in New York City is a population count, not a risk measure, and the 2005 metropolitan LGB figures are two decades old.

Whether Nassau County's 2025 ruling will survive the pending NYCLU litigation is unresolved in the inventory.

The April 2022 insurance-coverage lawsuit by a male same-sex couple over IVF and surrogacy coverage has no documented outcome in the inventory.

How New York's shield statutes interact with federal healthcare funding restrictions and federal enforcement pressure after January 2025 is not addressed in the inventory.
